_meta.note: Regression reference for Justify My Meeting (renamed from Meeting BS Detector, 2026-09-02 — the v1 goldens were discarded because they exercised eleven endpoints that no longer exist). Re-run with `npm run check:golden justify-my-meeting` against a local backend and diff for QUALITY, not exact match. Beyond what check-golden asserts automatically, eyeball these by hand, because no gate sees them: (1) every number in every prose field must trace to something the visitor supplied — the arithmetic lives in timeFootprint()/totals and nowhere else; (2) `verdict`, `better_format.recommendation` and `per_meeting[].read` must be EXACTLY the English enum strings, since the frontend looks them up to pick a colour and a t() key; (3) nothing may tell the visitor they are allowed to skip, and no message may announce rather than propose. Each case carries its own `guards` line saying what it is there to catch. See audit/tool-notes/JUSTIFYMYMEETING-NOTES.md.

cases.name: judge-with-numbers
cases.guards: person_hours must equal duration x attendees (22), computed in code. Plus the overreaches the two 2026-09-03 passes removed, every one of which the model produced here before: no generalising the visitor's own 90 seconds to the room; no reading recurrence as habit or lack of redesign; no reading no-prep as low engagement OR as evidence that advance thought is unnecessary; no treating the headcount as a verdict on who belongs — where contribution is unknown, it must SAY it is unknown whether everyone needs to attend. what_earns_the_meeting must be established or explicitly conditional, must not call the discussion contested, and must say something is LIKELY TO BENEFIT from real-time exchange rather than that it cannot happen async.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.context: I am one of the team leads. I speak for about 90 seconds and listen for the rest.

output.one_liner: Twenty-two people assembled to hear things they could have read is a ritual, not a meeting.
what_we_know: The meeting runs 60 minutes, weekly, with 22 attendees.
The agenda is status reports from each team lead.
No preparation is required of attendees.
No decisions are described as part of the format.
The visitor speaks for roughly 90 seconds and listens for the remainder.
The meeting has recurred for six months.
why_this_verdict: The described format is report-out only — the input does not establish that live back-and-forth, questioning, or coordination happens after or between updates.
The input does not establish how the other attendees use their time during reports; it is unknown whether discussion, escalation, or cross-team coordination occurs.
Preparation is not part of the described value, so the case for synchronous time has to rest entirely on what happens live — and the description does not supply that.
The meeting recurs, which makes it worth asking whether the format has been revisited, but recurrence alone establishes nothing about whether it is well-designed or stagnant.
what_earns_the_meeting: If team leads surface blockers or dependencies during updates, real-time exchange could allow immediate cross-team coordination that a written thread would resolve more slowly.

A standing all-hands may create shared awareness across teams that each lead would not otherwise have — this is a legitimate benefit if the content of other teams' updates is genuinely useful to attendees.
what_weakens_the_case: A format described purely as reporting out gives synchronous time no structural advantage over a shared written update — the back-and-forth that justifies live attendance is not described.
No decisions are part of the described format, removing one of the clearest justifications for assembling 22 people.

The visitor's own experience — 90 seconds speaking, the rest listening — suggests the meeting may deliver low active value to at least some attendees, though the input does not establish whether this holds for others.
unknowns_that_matter: Whether live discussion, questions, or coordination actually follow the updates — this is the most important unknown, and it could shift the verdict.
Whether the content of other teams' updates is genuinely useful to all 22 attendees, or primarily relevant to a subset.
Whether a written format has been tried or rejected for a specific reason.

better_format.how: Replace the standing slot with a shared weekly written update from each team lead; preserve a shorter live meeting — perhaps 20 to 30 minutes — only for weeks when something genuinely needs real-time discussion, coordination, or a decision.
better_format.assumptions: Team leads would actually write and read the updates; the organisation has a tool where async updates are visible to all attendees.

output.next_move: Raise the question with whoever owns the meeting: ask whether live discussion or coordination happens after the updates, and if not, propose a one-month trial of async updates with a short standing slot reserved for weeks that need it.
if_it_has_to_happen: Replace open-ended report-outs with a tight format: each lead gets 60 to 90 seconds, then flags one cross-team dependency or blocker — everything else goes in a written summary circulated before the meeting.
Reserve the final 10 to 15 minutes exclusively for live discussion on flagged items, and end early if nothing has been flagged.
Revisit the attendee list — if it is unknown whether all 22 people need the live content, that is a question worth putting to the group directly.

cases.name: judge-no-numbers
cases.guards: No duration, no headcount. time_footprint all-null, and no field may state a figure ABOUT THE MEETING that was not supplied. Numbers inside a PROPOSAL are fine — the line is claim versus suggestion, not the presence of a digit.

input.meetingText: Recurring 'project sync' with no agenda in the invite. In practice the organiser talks through a slide deck and asks at the end whether anyone has questions. Usually nobody does.

output.one_liner: A slide deck and a silent room is a presentation pretending to be a meeting.
what_we_know: The meeting recurs under the label 'project sync'
No agenda appears in the invite
In practice the organiser presents a slide deck
Questions are invited at the end
why_this_verdict: The described format is one-directional: the organiser presents, attendees receive — no exchange is built into the structure
The absence of end questions may mean the content is clear, or that attendees do not feel invited to push back — the input does not establish which
Preparation is not part of the described value, so the case for synchronous time has to rest on what happens live — and what is described live is a deck read-through
The meeting recurs, which makes it worth asking whether the format has been revisited — recurrence alone does not establish that it has not
what_earns_the_meeting: A recurring sync can create a reliable moment for questions, flags, and course corrections that might not otherwise surface — the current format does not appear to be using that potential
what_weakens_the_case: A slide deck covering project status can be shared asynchronously; the content as described does not require real-time delivery
When questions are routinely not asked, it is worth asking whether the live Q&A slot is doing any work at all
No agenda means attendees arrive without knowing what, if anything, they are expected to contribute
unknowns_that_matter: How many people attend, and whether any of them have roles that require coordination or shared decision-making
Whether the deck ever surfaces issues that lead to discussion — the input describes the typical case, not every case
Whether attendees have a channel to raise blockers or questions outside this meeting

better_format.how: Share the slide deck before the meeting with a short note inviting people to flag questions or blockers in writing. Hold the live session only if something needs to be talked through — otherwise cancel it that week.
better_format.assumptions: Attendees are willing to engage with a shared document before the scheduled slot, and there is somewhere to put written responses.

output.next_move: Ask the organiser — or yourself, if you are the organiser — what the meeting would lose if the deck were simply sent by email the day before.
if_it_has_to_happen: Drop the deck-walkthrough and open with a standing prompt: what is blocked, what has changed, what does the group need to decide — keep the organiser as facilitator, not presenter
End the meeting the moment no live discussion is happening — do not fill the slot because it was booked

cases.name: zombie
cases.guards: Weekly + duration + attendees, so occurrences_per_year (52) and annual_person_hours (156) come from PER_YEAR in code. what_would_be_lost holds established value or explicitly conditional possibilities only — no invented informal coordination, soft accountability or cohesion, and nothing inferred from people joining from their cars.

input.originalPurpose: Set up when we were launching the new site — we needed everyone in one place daily while things were breaking.
input.whatActuallyHappens: The site launched fourteen months ago. Now it is six people reading their Asana tasks aloud. Two people join from their cars.

output.one_liner: This meeting outlived its reason to exist fourteen months ago and is now six people reading a project management tool aloud.
output.then_and_now: It was created for daily crisis coordination during a site launch. The site launched fourteen months ago and the meeting now consists of attendees reciting their Asana tasks.
what_would_be_lost: Nothing specific was established from what you told me. That does not mean the meeting provides no value; it means any value beyond what you described is unknown.

what_to_change.why: The original purpose no longer exists, and reading Asana tasks aloud replicates information that is already written down

what_to_change.change: Replace with an async check-in only if team coordination still requires it
what_to_change.why: If there is genuine weekly coordination work, that need should be established before rebuilding the meeting in any form

unknowns_that_matter: Whether any live coordination, escalation, or decision-making actually happens that you did not describe
Whether the team has flagged any ongoing need for a shared weekly touchpoint
Whether the two people joining from cars are doing so by choice or because attendance feels obligatory despite the meeting having no clear value for them
output.next_move: Cancel it for four weeks, tell the team explicitly why, and see whether anything breaks or whether anyone asks for it back.

cases.name: zombie-no-original-purpose
cases.guards: then_and_now must NAME the missing purpose rather than inventing one, and must not read its absence as evidence the meeting is dead.

input.whatActuallyHappens: Someone shares a dashboard and asks if anyone has questions. It ends 20 minutes early most weeks.

output.one_liner: A dashboard someone could email, dressed up as a meeting.
output.then_and_now: The original purpose was not supplied. What happens now is one person shares a dashboard, asks for questions, and the group typically disperses 20 minutes early.
what_synchronous_still_does: Provides a moment where questions can be raised out loud, if anyone has them
what_would_be_lost: Nothing specific was established from what you told me. That does not mean the meeting provides no value; it means any value beyond what you described is unknown.

what_to_change.change: Replace the recurring slot with a shared dashboard link and an open invitation to flag questions asynchronously
what_to_change.why: The described format is one-way information delivery that regularly ends early, which suggests the live hour is not being used

what_to_change.change: If a live touchpoint still seems worth keeping, cut the slot to 20 minutes and make it optional
what_to_change.why: The meeting already runs about 40 minutes in practice; the scheduled hour creates overhead without described benefit

what_to_change.change: Clarify whether any cross-functional coordination or decisions are supposed to happen here
what_to_change.why: If that purpose exists but is not surfacing, the format may need a redesign rather than just a cancellation

unknowns_that_matter: Whether questions ever do get raised live that lead to meaningful discussion or decisions
Whether the 11 attendees are required or could opt in only when the data is relevant to them
Whether there is a coordination or escalation purpose that is not reflected in what actually happens
output.next_move: Pilot canceling one occurrence, share the dashboard by email instead, and see whether anything surfaces that would have required the room.

cases.name: week
cases.guards: One per_meeting entry per supplied meeting. `read` pinned to exact English and `name` pinned in code to the supplied name — one run copied the whole rendered list line into the field the frontend prints as the card heading. The 1:1 has no purpose supplied, so it MUST be 'not enough to tell': supplying the conventional purpose of a 1:1 and grading against it is the failure this case exists to catch. No `why` may say something cannot be done async. totals computed in code: 3.5h, 37 person-hours, 1 meeting missing numbers. summary carries no counts or ranges.

meetings.name: Monday standup
meetings.purpose: What everyone is working on this week

meetings.name: Design review
meetings.purpose: Decide whether the checkout flow ships

output.summary: A mix of recurring operational rhythm, a recurring decision gate, a one-off planning session, and a standing all-hands — spanning from small focused groups to a large gathering whose shape is not yet known.

per_meeting.name: Monday standup
per_meeting.why: The stated purpose is awareness sharing, which can benefit from real-time exchange if it surfaces blockers or coordination needs on the spot — but the input does not establish whether that exchange happens, so the case for keeping it live rests entirely on what occurs beyond the status update itself.

per_meeting.name: Design review
per_meeting.why: A ship/no-ship decision on a specific flow is the kind of call that is likely to benefit from real-time exchange — competing views, edge-case questions, and final alignment are easier to resolve when people can respond to each other directly.

per_meeting.name: Quarterly planning kickoff
per_meeting.why: Setting priorities for a quarter involves trade-offs that typically require live negotiation, and a kickoff creates shared commitment that is harder to build through a document or thread alone.

per_meeting.name: All-hands
per_meeting.why: No duration, attendee count, or purpose was supplied, so there is no basis to judge whether this meeting earns its time or how large its footprint is.

opportunities.change: Move status updates async before the standup, reserving live time only for coordination and blockers
opportunities.what_it_assumes: Attendees will actually read and post updates before the meeting, and the meeting has a facilitator willing to redirect status-reporting in real time

opportunities.change: Narrow attendance to decision-makers and direct contributors
opportunities.what_it_assumes: Some of the fourteen attendees are present for awareness rather than input, and that awareness can be delivered through a follow-up summary

opportunities.change: Shorten the standup if async updates are adopted — the live portion may not need its full slot
opportunities.what_it_assumes: The coordination and blocker discussion that justifies the live meeting takes less time than the full current slot

output.shape_of_the_week: No timing was supplied for any meeting beyond day name, so concentration or fragmentation across the week cannot be assessed.
unknowns_that_matter: What actually happens in the Monday standup beyond status sharing — whether it surfaces blockers or drives coordination
The all-hands duration, attendee count, and purpose, which determine whether it is the week's largest time investment
Whether any of the fourteen people in the quarterly kickoff are there for awareness only rather than active input
output.next_move: Find out what the all-hands is for and how long it runs — that is the one meeting whose footprint and value are entirely unknown.

cases.name: rescue
cases.guards: Role is 'Attending', so nothing may assume authority to end, leave or restructure. softer_version must not assume a separate conversation will be scheduled or that anyone wants one. after_the_meeting must be something THEY do.

input.whatsHappening: We are 35 minutes into a 45-minute meeting and we have not reached the thing it was called for. Two people are relitigating a decision that was made last month.

output.the_problem: With 10 minutes left, the meeting has not reached its stated purpose because two attendees are re-opening a decision already made last month.
output.say_this_now: Can we pause here — we have about 10 minutes left and have not gotten to the thing this meeting was called for. Can we set this aside and get to that now?
output.softer_version: I want to make sure we get to the reason we are all here before the time runs out — would it help to park this thread and decide as a group whether it needs its own time separately?
output.if_youre_not_running_it: You can address the room rather than the two people: something like 'I am conscious we are almost out of time and have not hit the main agenda item yet — is anyone else in the same place?'
output.if_its_time_to_wrap: If the original item cannot be covered in the remaining time, name that plainly: 'We are out of runway to do this properly — what is the right next step, and who owns it?'
output.after_the_meeting: Send a short note to whoever called the meeting noting that the original agenda item was not reached and asking how they want to handle it — that surfaces the gap without assuming a resolution.

cases.name: agenda-after-fix-it
cases.guards: The follow-up a FIX IT verdict earns, and the case that catches the agenda arguing against the old meeting instead of designing the new one. No field may criticise the existing format, invent blockers, dependencies or decisions, or describe what attendees already know. Any role the visitor did not supply must read as a design recommendation ('someone willing to capture decisions'), never as an existing post ('the note-taker'). why_live must phrase the live case as benefit, never impossibility. live_agenda minutes may total well under the duration — padding the slot right after recommending a shorter meeting is the contradiction this guards.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.context: I am one of the team leads. I speak for about 90 seconds and listen for the rest.

output.why_are_we_meeting: To surface anything that needs the whole engineering group to hear, respond to, or decide together — things that crossed team boundaries, created dependencies, or raised questions no single team can resolve alone. Status that requires no response stays out of the room.
what_must_be_true_when_we_leave: Any cross-team dependency or blocker that surfaced has an owner and a next step
Any question that needed the group has been answered or explicitly parked with an owner
Everyone who needs to know something learned it through exchange, not a broadcast
who_needs_to_participate: Each team lead — only to speak to anything their team raised that needs the group; not to report what the group does not need to act on

Someone with authority to make or unblock a decision if one surfaces — this role is not established in the input, but if no one present can say yes to anything, the meeting cannot close the loop it opens
Someone to capture decisions and owners before the meeting ends — this function is not established in the input and would need to be assigned
before_the_meeting: Each team lead posts a written update covering what their team did and any flag they want the group to address — so live time opens on flags, not on orientation
Attendees read the updates and mark anything they want to discuss, so the live agenda is known before anyone walks in

live_agenda.why_live: Takes ten seconds per item; faster to call them out verbally than to manage a shared doc in real time

live_agenda.item: Work through each flagged item: surface the dependency, disagreement, or question; reach a decision or assign an owner
live_agenda.why_live: Back-and-forth surfaces constraints and tradeoffs that a comment thread tends to drag out across days

live_agenda.item: If no flags were raised, the meeting does not need to convene — send a one-line message confirming that and give everyone the hour back
live_agenda.why_live: N/A — this is the condition under which live time is not warranted

output.end_with: Before the call ends, read back every decision, owner, and next step out loud — anything unresolved gets an explicit owner and a deadline, not a vague promise to follow up

cases.name: message-after-make-it-async
cases.guards: The follow-up a MAKE IT ASYNC verdict earns. The message proposes, never announces, and never says the visitor will skip. why_it_lands explains the message's STRUCTURE — what it leads with, concedes, asks for, leaves open — and must never predict the recipient's reaction: not that they will agree, appreciate it, or feel less defensive. That is a claim about a person nobody has met.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.better: Written updates from each lead before a deadline, plus a 20-minute sync kept only for what needs live discussion.

output.message: I wanted to share an idea about the weekly all-hands that I think could give everyone more time back. What if each lead submitted a short written update by, say, end of day Monday, and we kept a 20-minute sync on Tuesday for anything that actually needs the group live? I think we would cover the same ground with less time cost, and the written updates would be easier to reference later. Would you be open to piloting it for a few weeks?
output.why_it_lands: It leads with a concrete proposal rather than a complaint, frames the change as a gain for everyone rather than a personal preference, asks for a limited trial rather than a permanent commitment, and leaves the decision entirely with the manager.
output.if_they_say_no: Acknowledge the response and ask what the meeting is solving that the proposed format would not — that keeps the conversation open without pressing the point.
output.do_not_send: Any version that describes the current meeting as a waste of time costs the relationship, because it implies the manager has been running something indefensible for six months.
